section_summary: This section contains despatches and press enclosures from the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo dating from February 1937, reporting on internal political turbulence under Premier Senjuro Hayashi's newly formed cabinet. It covers contentious interpellations in the reconvened Imperial Diet concerning the Army's interference in civilian politics, surging military spending at the expense of agrarian and economic relief, and diplomatic policies toward China and the Soviet Union, highlighting an outspoken speech by liberal parliamentarian Yukio Ozaki. In addition, the section analyzes a developing rightist movement led by retired officers and nationalists seeking to dissolve traditional parliamentary parties and create a totalitarian unified party under the Japanese Imperial Way.

subfiles.about: Report on interpellations in the 70th Imperial Diet criticizing Army interference in politics, military budgets, and foreign policy toward China and the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 2271 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports on opening interpellations in the House of Peers and House of Representatives on February 15 and 16, 1937. Diet members from the Minseito and Seiyukai challenged the Hayashi Cabinet regarding the Army's role in toppling the Hirota Cabinet, the blocking of General Ugaki's attempt to form a cabinet, and the ballooning defense budget compared to neglected rural relief. Government ministers, including War Minister Sugiyama, Navy Minister Yonai, and Finance Minister Yuki, gave restrained and conciliatory responses, with Yuki frankly acknowledging budget and bond absorption difficulties while seeking a middle road between Takahashi and Baba. The despatch is prefaced by a State Department summary sheet and accompanied by press clippings from The Japan Times and The Japan Advertiser detailing the debates.
subfiles.title: Interpellations in the Opening Diet Sessions of February 15 and 16

subfiles.about: Analysis of the rightist and military-backed movement to organize a single totalitarian nationalist political party to displace traditional parliamentary parties in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 2273 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew examines the growing movement among right-wing elements, retired military officers, and reactionary societies to form a unified nationalist party supported by the Army. The initiative was driven by intense friction between military authorities and the established political parties (Seiyukai, Minseito, and Social Masses Party), as well as demands to place the national economy on a semi-wartime footing in preparation for potential war. Key figures such as Colonel Kingoro Hashimoto, Lieutenant-General Yoshiji Tatekawa, and Mitsuru Toyama led organizations like the Nippon Seinen-to and Ishin Seido Kenkyu-kai advocating 'Nippon Shugi' (the Japanese principle) and the Imperial Way. The embassy observed that while the movement drew inspiration from European fascism and possessed strong destructive intent toward party government, it suffered from vague ideology, lack of concrete economic policies, and factional instability.
subfiles.title: New Party Movement in Japan

subfiles.about: Transmittal and press report of an aggressive parliamentary interpellation by veteran liberal Yukio Ozaki condemning military interference in government, defense expansion, and the Anti-Comintern Pact.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 2274 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits a detailed press account from The Japan Advertiser covering proceedings in the House of Representatives on February 17, 1937, dominated by a 105-minute speech by veteran independent parliamentarian Yukio Ozaki. Ozaki asserted that no external crisis existed in the Far East to justify staggering armament increases, denounced the Anti-Comintern agreement with Nazi Germany as foolish and counterproductive, urged peaceful conciliation with China and the Soviet Union, and severely rebuked the military for meddling in civil politics and foreign affairs. War Minister Sugiyama defended the Army by claiming political corruption was the motive behind the February 26 Incident, and other Diet members interpellated cabinet ministers over state control of industry and soaring commodity prices. The despatch is prefaced by an internal State Department Far Eastern Affairs docket slip.
subfiles.title: Interpellation by Mr. Yukio Ozaki
